papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: In locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC), neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NCIT) plus high-quality surgery (R0 resection with systematic lymphadenectomy >19 nodes) is a promising strategy. However, the value of adjuvant immunotherapy remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy and survival outcomes in a multicenter cohort. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study enrolled LA-ESCC patients receiving NCIT from eight high-volume Chinese centers between 2019 and 2023. After screening for high-quality surgery, propensity score matching (PSM) balanced characteristics between the two groups: NCIT plus surgery (NCIT+S) and NCIT plus surgery followed by adjuvant immunotherapy (NCIT+S+ICI). The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). A prognostic framework based on major pathological response (MPR) and postoperative pathological N stage (ypN) was constructed to refine patient selection. RESULTS: Among 724 patients with a median follow-up of 40.3 months, 3-year OS and DFS rates were 73.0% and 67.7%, respectively. After PSM, adjuvant immunotherapy significantly improved DFS (77.1% vs 65.8%, log-rank P=0.037), but not OS (83.4% vs 69.4%, log-rank P=0.058). Multivariate analysis identified ypN, MPR, and postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy as independent prognostic factors for DFS. Stratification by MPR and ypN status showed that DFS benefit from adjuvant immunotherapy was restricted to the non-MPR/ypN+ subgroup (HR=0.339; 95% CI: 0.173-0.662; log-rank P<0.001), with a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction (P for interaction=0.025). CONCLUSIONS: Among LA-ESCC patients receiving NCIT and high-quality surgery, adjuvant immunotherapy significantly improves 3-year DFS in the non-MPR/ypN+ subgroup, with no significant benefit in other subgroups.

papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: To develop quality assurance models for adverse procedural events after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer. METHODS: Using procedural outcomes after 16,430 lung resections and 3,068 esophagectomies for cancer at 9 hospitals in 7 hospital systems, we developed 5 individual and 2 composite outcome models from preoperative information. Random forest quantile classification for imbalanced data with model-free variable priority screening identified predictors. Out-of-bag prediction provided regularized estimates and internal validation. Hospital-holdout analysis assessed institutional benchmark stability. RESULTS: Of 71 lung resection and 63 esophagectomy preoperative variables, 35 and 29, respectively, were identified as important predictors across the 7 outcome models. These included demographics, advanced cancer, organ dysfunction, higher acuity, and planned surgical approach and resection extent. Out-of-bag calibration covered a modest range of probabilities. Out-of-bag geometric mean ranged from 0.588 to 0.713 for lung resection and 0.517 to 0.649 for esophagectomy. Continuous risk factors, particularly pulmonary function, provided high-importance information content, with complex dependency and interaction structure among predictors. Risk-factor magnitude differed among hospitals, as did their risk-adjusted outcomes according to patient risk as determined by counterfactual inference within a framework of virtual twins. For lung resection operative mortality, hospital-specific contrasts were stable when each focal hospital was excluded from the aggregate benchmark. CONCLUSIONS: Using contemporary machine learning, initial models for adverse procedural events after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer have been developed. They provide surgeons, their patients, and hospital and hospital systems tools for patient risk assessment and for informing quality improvement initiatives in general thoracic surgery.

papers.abstract_en: Gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEAC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy with limited effective targeted therapies. Cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9), a key regulator of transcriptional elongation, has been implicated in oncogenic processes across multiple cancer types; however, its functional role and therapeutic potential in GEAC remain poorly defined. In this study, we systematically investigated CDK9 expression, function, and therapeutic targeting in GEAC, with particular emphasis on its interaction with the YAP/TEAD signaling axis. Immunohistochemical analysis of primary GEAC tumors and patient-derived xenografts revealed elevated CDK9 expression, which correlated with poor patient survival. Mechanistic studies using immunofluorescence and co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated a reciprocal regulatory interaction between CDK9 and YAP1, promoting transcriptional programs associated with tumor progression and radiation resistance. We developed novel CDK9-targeting proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and identified YX0597 as a potent CDK9 degrader. YX0597 effectively suppressed RNAP II Ser2 phosphorylation (RNAP II P-S2) and downregulated oncogenic drivers, including MCL-1. Functionally, CDK9 degradation markedly inhibited GEAC cell proliferation, invasion, and tumor sphere formation, with enhanced efficacy in radiation-resistant cells. Integrated RNA sequencing and ATAC sequencing revealed that CDK9 degradation increased chromatin accessibility, reactivated epigenetically silenced genes, and profoundly suppressed YAP/TEAD transcriptional activity. These coordinated transcriptional and epigenetic alterations disrupted oncogenic homeostasis, resulting in broad cytotoxicity. Importantly, co-targeting CDK9 and YAP/TEAD signaling produced strong synergistic antitumor effects in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our findings identify CDK9 as a critical oncogenic driver in GEAC and highlight CDK9 degradation, particularly in combination with YAP/TEAD inhibition, as a promising therapeutic strategy for refractory GEAC.

papers.abstract_en: While immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized treatment of the patients with aero-upper digestive squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs), including esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), only a subset of patients benefit from ICIs, therefore entailing exploration of the mechanisms to regulate treatment responsiveness. POLE, as a subunit of DNA polymerase ε, possesses 3'-5' proofreading activity, and its mutations have been associated with favourable response to ICIs in several solid tumors. However, post-translational modification (PTM) of POLE and its impact on the therapeutic efficacy of ICIs are unknown. Here, this study demonstrates that ubiquitin-like protein 3 (Ubl3), whose expression is markedly downregulated in SCCs, covalently binds to Pole, reduces nuclear Pole levels, triggers DNA damage, and activates cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Notably, Ubl3 modification of Pole significantly primes the local immune microenvironment to mitigate the growth of murine aero-upper digestive SCC cells and boost the efficacy of αPD-1 treatment in vivo. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis further revealed that UBL3 expression is positively correlated with better clinical outcomes in a cohort of ESCC patients receiving neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with αPD-1. Together, our findings unravel UBL3 modification as a novel PTM mechanism governing subcellular location of POLE and its influence on immunotherapy responsiveness, thus making UBL3 modification as a promising immunomodulatory approach to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in patients with aero-upper digestive SCCs.

papers.abstract_en: Patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) have an unmet need for new therapies that improve survival. In this phase II trial, patients received ociperlimab and tislelizumab (A) or placebo and tislelizumab (B) (NCT04732494). The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) assessed by the investigator per RECIST v1.1. A total of 125 patients were randomized to A (N = 62) and B (N = 63). The primary endpoint was not met, with an ORR (95% confidence interval [CI]) assessed by the investigator of 30.6% (19.6-43.7) for A and 20.6% (11.5-32.7) for B (stratified risk difference: 9.9% [95% CI - 5.4 to 25.3]; stratified 2-sided p = 0.2114). At the final analysis, median OS (95% CI) was 10.2 (7.9-19.5) months for A and 9.3 (6.4-14.8) months for B (stratified HR [95% CI]: 0.92 [0.58-1.45]). A total of 25.8% (16/62) and 20.6% (13/63) of patients in A and B, respectively, experienced grade ≥3 treatment-related treatment-emergent adverse events. Exploratory biomarker analyses showed that patients with an inflamed tumor microenvironment, shown by the enriched expression of natural killer (NK) cells, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and B-cell signatures, and NK cell signature enrichment, may benefit from ociperlimab plus tislelizumab. Adding ociperlimab to tislelizumab did not provide significant efficacy improvement in recurrent/metastatic second-line ESCC; the addition of ociperlimab to tislelizumab was generally well-tolerated. Trial registration: Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT04732494.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: The tumor suppressor TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer, and drugs targeting specific mutant p53 proteins have been developed. Rezatapopt, which reactivates the Y220C p53 protein, was recently evaluated in the Phase I PYNNACLE trial in patients with solid tumors, with promising results. The trial did not enrol any non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cases, and little is known about the clinicopathological characteristics and genetic profile of the TP53 Y220C NSCLC patients. METHODS: In this multicenter, European Thoracic Oncology Platform-sponsored study, we retrospectively collected data from NSCLC patients from several European institutions with Next Generation Sequencing data available. papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Lung-protective ventilation is essential in the management of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), but current approaches are limited by the heterogeneity of lung pathology and a lack of individualized strategies. papers.abstract_en: Tumor heterogeneity is a universal feature of cancer and may arise as early as precancer stages during lung adenocarcinoma evolution, yet the emergence of aggressive transcriptional programs remains incompletely understood. Here, we integrated spatial transcriptomics with single-cell RNA sequencing to characterize inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity across hyperplasia, adenoma, and invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) in a genetically engineered mouse model (129S4/Sv KrasLSL-G12D/+). Together, these findings indicate that aggressive transcriptional divergence can emerge early during lung adenocarcinoma evolution and that spatial organization critically shapes tumor and immune programs before and after invasion.

papers.abstract_en: Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) develop from the stratified epithelia of the esophagus, head and neck, lung, and skin, providing a tractable model to investigate how altered epithelial fields progress toward invasive cancer. Across SCC subtypes, evolution often begins before overt malignancy, with age- and exposure-associated mutant clones expanding within histologically normal epithelia. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in the temporal ordering and spatial patterning of SCC evolution and discuss how genetic alterations, epigenetic remodeling, and tissue ecology jointly drive disease progression. We further highlight the implications for early interception, biomarker development, immune evasion, and evolution-informed prevention and therapy.

papers.abstract_en: Mycobacterium abscessus (Mab) is a rapidly growing non-tuberculous mycobacterium that causes opportunistic infections and exhibits extensive intrinsic antibiotic resistance. The proline-glutamate (PE) and proline-proline-glutamate (PPE) protein families are mycobacteria-specific virulence factors implicated in immune modulation, antigenic variation, and persistence. While Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) harbors approximately 170 PE/PPE members, the repertoire of PE/PPE genes in Mab remains largely uncharacterized. Here, we performed a genome-wide survey of PE/PPE genes in Mab ATCC 19,977 and identified 18 candidate family members, representing a relatively small fraction of the genome compared with slow-growing mycobacteria. Most predicted proteins harbor canonical PE or PPE domains and display acidic physicochemical properties. Phylogenetic analysis resolved the proteins into three subfamilies: PE, PPE, and PE-PPE, revealing moderate structural diversity but limited family expansion. Motif and gene structure analyses supported the evolutionary conservation. Notably, no PE_polymorphic GC-rich repetitive sequence (PE_PGRS) or PPE_major polymorphic tandem repeat (PPE_MPTR) members were detected, suggesting lineage-specific genomic reduction relative to other pathogenic mycobacteria. AlphaFold predictions revealed conserved N-terminal folds and variable C-terminal regions, which may contribute to functional diversification. Subcellular localization predictions indicated that most proteins are extracellular. Synteny analysis revealed no detectable collinearity among these genes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed condition-dependent expression of PE/PPE genes during amoeba and macrophage infection and under artificial sputum medium and metal ion stress, suggesting roles in environmental adaptation and host interaction. This study provides the first systematic overview of PE/PPE gene repertoire in Mab and lays the groundwork for elucidating their roles in intracellular survival, host interaction, and antimicrobial resistance.

papers.abstract_en: The etiology of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remains unknown, and therapeutic interventions are currently restricted. papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary carcinoids generally have favorable outcomes after surgery, but postoperative recurrence differs substantially by histological subtype. Existing guidance recognizes atypical histology and nodal involvement as adverse features, yet a focused quantitative synthesis of the magnitude and consistency of this association remains limited. METHODS: MEDLINE/PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to July 12, 2026 for surgical cohorts reporting postoperative recurrence. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full-text eligibility, with disagreements resolved by consensus. The primary meta-analysis emphasized the risk ratio (RR) of observed recurrence in atypical versus typical carcinoids using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood and modified Hartung-Knapp intervals; odds ratios (ORs) and risk differences were complementary measures. Time-defined recurrence, adjusted prognostic factors, and anatomical patterns were synthesized separately because of incompatible outcome definitions and effect measures. RESULTS: Eighteen reports were included in the review, 11 contributed structured quantitative evidence, and 7 independent comparative cohorts entered the primary meta-analysis. Among 1074 resected tumors, recurrence occurred in 24 of 816 typical carcinoids and 51 of 258 atypical carcinoids. The pooled RR of observed recurrence was 6.57 (95% CI, 3.65-11.84), with a complementary OR of 8.08 (95% CI, 4.20-15.53). No statistical heterogeneity was detected (I2 = 0%), but this result was interpreted cautiously because only seven studies were available and clinically important differences in follow-up, staging, pathological review, and surveillance remained. Leave-one-out RR estimates ranged from 5.77 to 7.48. Time-defined evidence suggested recurrence of approximately 18%-25% by 5 years and 29%-32% by 10 years in atypical tumors, whereas node-negative typical tumors generally remained below 5% at 10 years, although late events occurred. Nodal involvement, advanced pT category, and larger tumor size were adverse prognostic features. CONCLUSION: Observed recurrence after resection was substantially more frequent in atypical than in typical pulmonary carcinoids. Histology and nodal status provide a clinically useful basis for postoperative risk stratification, but the available evidence does not establish the optimal surveillance modality, interval, or duration.

papers.abstract_en: Four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT) is routinely used in radiotherapy simulation to evaluate respiration-induced tumor motion, but the motion information is often reviewed visually rather than captured as structured, phase-resolved data. We developed and evaluated M4DTrack, a DICOM-based imaging-informatics workflow for user-supervised 4DCT lung tumor motion analysis and structured, exportable three-dimensional center-of-mass (CoM) motion reporting. M4DTrack imports phase-resolved DICOM CT images, groups images by respiratory phase, displays linked axial/coronal/sagittal views, supports crosshair-based tumor localization and HU inspection, and applies seed or linked 3D-box initialization with sequential phase-to-phase HU-volume propagation. An 8-case lower-lobe lung 4DCT dataset (80 respiratory phases) was analyzed. Directional amplitudes, 3D vector amplitude, maximum phase-wise displacement, and agreement with independent ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were quantified. HU-weighted CoM amplitudes were 2.44 ± 1.44 mm, 2.64 ± 1.37 mm, and 6.04 ± 2.48 mm in X, Y, and Z patient-coordinate directions, respectively. Mean 3D vector amplitude was 7.26 ± 2.50 mm, and mean maximum phase-wise 3D displacement was 6.20 ± 2.10 mm. Biases versus ITV-GTV reference amplitudes were 0.01, - 0.84, and 0.23 mm for X, Y, and Z, respectively, with a 3D vector amplitude bias of - 0.29 mm. M4DTrack provides a user-supervised imaging-informatics bridge between qualitative 4DCT cine review and structured quantitative motion documentation. The pilot results support feasibility for generating exportable, phase-resolved tumor-motion metrics while preserving user-supervised review of 4DCT artifacts, HU-capture uncertainty, adjacent anatomy, and differences between CoM-based and extent-based measurements.

papers.abstract_en: Accurate pulmonary nodule detection in computed tomography (CT) remains challenging because small- and low-contrast nodules may resemble vessels and other anatomical structures on individual axial slices. We propose 3D-DDN Faster R-CNN, a multi-slice detection framework that incorporates structured local axial context into a two-stage detector. The five-slice interactive blending (5-SIB) strategy organizes five consecutive CT slices as an ordered contextual group and preserves slice-specific feature streams extracted by a shared two-dimensional backbone. The cross-slice feature fusion (CSFF) module applies slice-wise spatial self-attention at shallow feature levels and learnable cross-slice aggregation at deep feature and region-of-interest levels. The dynamic displacement constraint (DDC) models proposal displacement across adjacent slices using a positive-sample regression loss and a margin-based negative-sample contrastive loss, while a class-weighted focal loss alleviates foreground-background imbalance. The model was evaluated on a private hospital dataset, LIDC-IDRI, and LNDb using patient-level data partitions. On the private hospital dataset, 3D-DDN achieved an average precision at an IoU threshold of 0.5 (AP0.5) of 75.80% ± 1.05%, a sensitivity of 89.33% ± 1.91%, and a competition performance metric (CPM) of 91.20% ± 1.50%. The corresponding AP0.5 values on LIDC-IDRI and LNDb were 66.27% ± 0.45% and 48.20% ± 0.30%, respectively. Ablation experiments showed that direct five-slice stacking degraded performance, whereas structured feature fusion and displacement supervision recovered the performance loss and improved the overall detection profile. These results indicate that ordered cross-slice representation, hierarchical feature fusion, and proposal-displacement supervision provide complementary mechanisms for incorporating local three-dimensional context.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Reduced exercise capacity, measured by the 6-min walk distance (6MWD), is a critical prognostic factor in interstitial lung disease (ILD). However, conventional physiological markers often fail to identify early functional decline. We aimed to evaluate whether the foot-to-foot lower-limb phase angle (F-F PhA), a non-invasive surrogate marker of muscle quality, predicts reduced exercise capacity better than traditional muscle mass and pulmonary function indices. Reduced exercise capacity was defined as 6MWD < 450 m. Multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age and pulmonary function (%DLCO or %FVC), with internal validation performed via 1000-resample bootstrapping. RESULTS: In multivariable analysis, F-F PhA was independently associated with a 6MWD < 450 m when adjusted for age and %DLCO (OR: 0.228, 95% CI: 0.088-0.591, p = 0.002; bootstrap p = 0.005) or %FVC (OR: 0.213, 95% CI: 0.091-0.496, p = 0.001; bootstrap p = 0.001). ROC analysis showed F-F PhA had the highest discriminative accuracy (AUC: 0.802), outperforming %DLCO (AUC: 0.729) and ESM_CSA (AUC: 0.701). Combining age, %DLCO, and F-F PhA achieved the highest performance (AUC: 0.833). CONCLUSIONS: F-F PhA serves as a robust, independent indicator for predicting reduced exercise capacity in ILD, outperforming conventional muscle mass. As a non-invasive tool, F-F PhA complements established functional tests in screening for early physical decline.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: By preserving spontaneous breathing and avoiding mechanical ventilation, Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery may attenuate perioperative inflammatory responses and promote early mobilization, thereby influencing the risk of venous thromboembolism. However, whether the risk of postoperative venous thromboembolism differs between Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and conventional Intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery remains unclear due to a lack of definitive evidence. We hypothesized that patients undergoing Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery would have a lower risk of postoperative venous thromboembolism. METHODS: A single-center retrospective study was conducted. Patients with lung cancer who underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic lung surgery at the Department of Cardiothoracic Surgery, Jinhua Central Hospital between March 2025 and July 2025 were enrolled and, based on the anesthetic approach, divided into the Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group (n = 25) and the Intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group (n = 30). The primary outcome was the risk of venous thromboembolism, as assessed by thrombotic complications, postoperative coagulation parameters, time to early postoperative ambulation, time to first flatus, and time to first defecation. RESULTS: No perioperative venous thromboembolic complications occurred in either group. Regarding coagulation parameters, the D-dimer level in the Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group was 0.30 (0.04, 0.70) µg/L, which was significantly lower than 0.77 (0.34, 1.46) µg/L in the I-VATS group (P = 0.006). There were no statistically significant differences in prothrombin time (PT) or activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) between the two groups (P > 0.05). The time to early postoperative ambulation was significantly shorter in the Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group [0 (0, 0) days] than in the Intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group [1 (1, 1) days] (P < 0.001). The time to first flatus and defecation was 1 (1, 1) day in the Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group, significantly shorter than 2 (2, 3) days in the Intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group (P < 0.001). Furthermore, the Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group exhibited a significantly attenuated elevation in the inflammatory marker (leukocyte count: 2.24 ± 0.39 × 10⁹/L) compared with the Intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery group (5.82 ± 0.60 × 10⁹/L). CONCLUSIONS: Non-intubated video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery may reduce the risk of venous thromboembolism through several mechanisms: maintaining negative intrathoracic pressure generated by spontaneous breathing, lowering the risk of elevated intra-abdominal pressure, and facilitating early mobilization - all of which enhance venous return; substituting general anesthesia with combined regional anesthesia; and avoiding muscle relaxants, thereby attenuating surgery-induced hypercoagulability and preserving endothelial function.

papers.abstract_en: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the most common subtype of lung cancer, is associated with substantial global mortality. Nuclear receptor coactivator 5 (NCOA5) has been implicated in several malignancies; however, its functional role and regulatory mechanisms in LUAD remain largely unknown. In this study, NCOA5 expression was evaluated in 94 paired LUAD and adjacent tissues using immunohistochemistry, RT-PCR, and Western blotting. Functional analyses were conducted using shRNA knockdown, CRISPR-mediated knockout, and overexpression models to assess the effects of NCOA5 on LUAD cell proliferation, migration, invasion, apoptosis, cell cycle progression, and organoid formation. Xenograft models were used to validate tumorigenicity in vivo. IP-MS and co-immunoprecipitation identified NCOA5-interacting proteins, while ChIP-seq and dual-luciferase assays interrogated downstream transcriptional regulation. NCOA5 was significantly upregulated in LUAD tissues and associated with advanced stage, poor differentiation, and reduced overall survival, serving as an independent prognostic factor (P < .040). NCOA5 knockdown inhibited LUAD cell proliferation, migration, invasion, induced G0/G1 arrest, promoted apoptosis, reduced organoid formation, and suppressed xenograft growth, whereas NCOA5 overexpression produced the opposite effects. Among 39 candidate interacting proteins identified by IP-MS, ZCCHC3 was validated as a direct NCOA5-binding partner. ZCCHC3 depletion phenocopied NCOA5 loss and reversed NCOA5-induced proliferation, migration, invasion, and colony formation, supporting a functional NCOA5-ZCCHC3 interaction. ChIP-seq analysis identified fibroblast growth factor 22 (FGF22) as a direct transcriptional target of NCOA5. FGF22 was markedly downregulated in LUAD tissues and higher FGF22 expression was associated with improved patient survival. NCOA5 suppressed FGF22 transcription, while NCOA5 inhibition increased FGF22 expression. Functionally, FGF22 knockdown enhanced LUAD aggressiveness, whereas FGF22 restoration abrogated the oncogenic effects of NCOA5 in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, these findings identify a previously unrecognized NCOA5-ZCCHC3/FGF22 axis that drives LUAD progression and provide new mechanistic insight into the role of NCOA5 in LUAD biology.

papers.abstract_en: Radiation-induced lung injury (RILI) is a common dose-limiting toxicity after radiotherapy for lung cancer, but the immunological mechanisms contributing to RILI pathogenesis remain poorly understood. Thus, our findings indicate that radiation-induced type I IFN induces ILC2-to-ILC1 plasticity to contribute to RILI pathogenesis, and suggest that targeting type I IFN signaling may be a therapeutic strategy to mitigate radiation-induced lung injury.

papers.abstract_en: INTRODUCTION: Tumor proximity to the left brachiocephalic vein (LBCV) may affect vascular exposure and dissection during the subxiphoid approach (SXA). papers.abstract_en: OBJECTIVE: To inform lung cancer screening (LCS) in primary care settings, the study assessed providers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices around LCS and recommended implementation strategies. METHODS: The online survey was administered from May-August 2025 among primary care providers in Georgia, USA. We ran descriptive analyses for all data and linear regression for predictors of greater knowledge. RESULTS: Providers (N = 112) had an average knowledge score of 3.72/5 (SD = 1.11). Physicians (N = 73) scored significantly higher than nurses/nurse practitioners (β = -1.0, 95% CI: -1.6, -0.44). Overall, participants viewed LCS positively, and about 45% reported offering LCS at their facility while 50% reported referring patients to LCS programs. Most (75.5%) had strategies to follow-up with patients who screened positive, but few (22.6%) offered tobacco cessation services. Top barriers were cost, lack of patient knowledge/interest, and transportation; cost assistance, patient education materials, and patient navigation were the top facilitators. Providers (N = 86) identified 'Distributing patient educational materials' and 'Reminding clinicians' as highly feasible and important implementation strategies. CONCLUSIONS: While most providers had sufficient knowledge, positive perceptions, and high availability of LCS services, few engage in patient education or offer smoking cessation resources. Patient education and clinician reminders may be beneficial implementation strategies for primary care-based LCS.

papers.abstract_en: With the increase in the diagnosis rate of small pulmonary nodules, the segmentectomy has been increasingly used in clinical practice worldwide. However, for the segmentectomy, the confirmation of intersegmental plane has always puzzled many thoracic surgeons. This paper described a new method, named artery-based Inflation-deflation method, used to confirm the intersegmental border under video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery. After only dividing the targeted segment artery and preserving the targeted segmental veins and bronchi, the intersegmental plane was successfully generated by this novel Inflation-deflation method. Compared with other current methods, this new technique had some advantages including the smaller airway damage, easier to determine the intersegmental plane, the higher fault-tolerant rate and easy to operate without any additional devices. And a further clinical study should be carried out to verify the feasibility and applicability of this new technique.

papers.abstract_en: BACKGROUND: Bronchogenic cysts are usually asymptomatic and are often detected incidentally; however, they may become symptomatic due to infection, hemorrhage, or enlargement. We report a case of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst that showed substantial enlargement from 4.8 to 13 cm over an 8-year interval, with intracystic hemorrhage, ultimately requiring partial resection of the esophageal muscularis. CASE PRESENTATION: A man in his 20s presented with upper abdominal pain and nausea. Computed tomography revealed a 13-cm mass extending from below the tracheal bifurcation to the level of the gastric cardia. A CT scan obtained eight years earlier during the evaluation of abdominal pain had shown a 4.8-cm cystic lesion below the tracheal bifurcation, demonstrating substantial enlargement over the intervening period. Although conservative treatment was attempted, compressive symptoms persisted; therefore, surgical resection was performed for definitive diagnosis and symptom relief. Severe inflammatory adhesions necessitated right open thoracotomy with partial resection of the esophageal muscularis. The cyst contained a large hematoma, and histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a bronchogenic cyst with intracystic hemorrhage. CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates substantial enlargement of a previously unrecognized bronchogenic cyst from 4.8 to 13 cm over an 8-year interval, with intracystic hemorrhage, symptomatic progression, and technically demanding surgical resection. The potential for substantial enlargement and increasing surgical complexity should be considered when determining the timing of resection for bronchogenic cysts.

papers.abstract_en: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is characterized by airflow limitation, dynamic hyperinflation, and intrinsic positive end-expiratory pressure (iPEEP), which increase inspiratory threshold load and complicate ventilatory support. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) is the preferred initial ventilatory support for COPD exacerbations complicated by acute or acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis, while invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) may be required when NIV fails. External PEEP may reduce the inspiratory threshold load in patients with expiratory flow limitation, although excessive levels can increase lung volume and compromise hemodynamics. During IMV, PEEP adjustment requires assessment of respiratory mechanics, expiratory flow, hyperinflation, and cardiovascular tolerance. During NIV, where iPEEP cannot usually be measured directly, expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP) should be adjusted according to clinical response, patient-ventilator interaction, and signs of excessive lung inflation. Inappropriate ventilatory assistance may also contribute to diaphragm dysfunction. Diaphragm ultrasound allows bedside assessment of muscle thickness and inspiratory thickening fraction (DTF), although these measurements are influenced by ventilatory assistance, respiratory drive, and lung volume. This review examines the physiological basis, available evidence, and limitations of using diaphragm ultrasound to complement PEEP adjustment in patients with COPD and dynamic hyperinflation. No DTF target or clinical benefit of ultrasound-guided PEEP titration has been established in this population.
